eight_day_check.verdict: NOT SUPPORTED by any official source. Official sources say ONE WEEK (7 days).
official_findings: gov.gr National Registry of Administrative Public Services (mitos.gov.gr), 'Issue of a marriage licence for foreign residents in Greece', last updated 5 Nov 2026: the mayor waits one week from the date the application is submitted for third-party objections; with no objection the licence is granted immediately after that week; completion deadline 7 days; fee EUR 18 (e-paravolo code 2386); validity 6 months; supporting documents include a CNI, a birth certificate translated into Greek, and the newspaper issue carrying the marriage announcement. Legal basis: Civil Code arts 1368 to 1370, Law 1250/1982, PD 391/1982; Law 5089/2024 for same-sex marriage.

Municipality of Athens, 'Issuance of Civil Marriage License': 'issued seven (7) days after the submission and verification of the required documents and is valid for six (6) months'; all documents issued within the last six months; announcement in a daily Athenian newspaper, with names also in Latin characters if a spouse is foreign. This page serves residents of Athens.

Municipality of Chania, 'Documents required for committing a civil marriage for foreigners residing abroad' (PDF): non-resident foreigners bring a marriage licence from their own country naming the intended spouse, translated and certified, plus birth certificate, family status certificate (if issued) and passport copy; apostille plus official Greek translation. No Greek licence or waiting period is described for non-residents.

Municipality of Heraklion, 'Marriage license for foreigner nationals': residents follow the licence route (CNI, newspaper notice, EUR 18 fee stamp); non-residents need a marriage licence from their country (apostilled, translated) and 'a residence permit or VISA'. Needs checking for visa-free Australians.

Australian Embassy Athens, 'Getting married in Greece': a CNI is required by religious and municipal bodies for each non-Greek citizen; lodge in Athens or at any DFAT office in Australia; acceptable place of issue differs between organisations; CNI issued in English and must be translated into Greek.

Smartraveller (DFAT), 'How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage', last updated 1 Oct 2026: issued by Passport Offices, missions overseas and by mail; ask the local authority whether it must be issued in-country and whether it needs an apostille.
eight_day_check.where_eight_comes_from: Commercial pages only: bigfatgreekday.com (AU and US guides) says '~8 days' and attributes it to the gov.gr registry page, which says 7 days; translayte.com says a newspaper notice must run 'at least 8 days before applying' and cites the same gov.gr page, which does not say that; a Scribd PDF says 'eight days post-application'. A plausible reading: submit on day 0, the one-week objection window runs, the licence is collected on day 8. That is our explanation to test, not a sourced fact.
eight_day_check.what_starts_the_clock: Submission of the complete application with all supporting documents (including the already-published newspaper notice) at the municipality. Athens says 'after submission and verification'. Incomplete files are returned and the procedure restarts (gov.gr steps 2 to 4).
eight_day_check.what_it_applies_to: The Greek municipal licence for foreigners resident in Greece (and Greek citizens). For couples resident abroad, municipalities differ: Chania and Heraklion describe accepting a home-country marriage licence instead. Australia does not issue a 'marriage licence'; the DFAT CNI is the usual substitute. The researcher must confirm with official sources whether a non-resident Australian couple goes through the 7-day licence at all, municipality by municipality.
eight_day_check.civil_vs_orthodox: gov.gr (mitos 'Issue of a civil marriage licence' entry, per search snippet) says the mayor's licence is required for civil marriage and for marriage solemnised by the Eastern Orthodox Church. Church requirements (baptism, Holy Metropolis approval, sponsor rules) sit on top and are not in any official page read. UNRESOLVED: researcher to confirm from an official church or government source.
exceptions_and_conflicts: Translation: the Australian Embassy page says Greece accepts only translations by the Greek MFA Translation Section or Greek consulates. The Ministry of Interior library lists 2021 circulars on the abolition of the MFA translation service and a 'new system of official translation'. Chania lists consulate, MFA translation service, Ionian University graduates or a Greek lawyer. Researcher must resolve which applies now.

Newspaper notice: required by gov.gr (residents) and Athens; Heraklion asks residents for a one-day notice in a named local daily. Not described for non-residents in Chania. 'Eight days before applying' is unsourced.
40-day registration after the ceremony: commercial sources only so far. Researcher to verify from an official source.
Same-sex marriage: legal since Law 5089/2024 (cited by gov.gr). One ranking venue page still says it is not.

cross_market_insights: Every market's SERP is weak: Facebook group threads take 2 or 3 of the top 3 in Sydney, Melbourne and Singapore, and the US query is hijacked by the Town of Greece, New York. There is no authoritative, Australian, officially sourced page in the top 10 anywhere.

People Also Ask is the same globally and US-skewed ('register my marriage in the U.S.'); the only Australian PAA is 'How long can an Australian citizen stay in Greece?'. A clean Australian answer to recognition at home and length of stay is open.

The 'eight days' figure is a meme repeated by commercial pages that cite gov.gr for a number gov.gr does not contain. Official sources say one week. A page that explains the real rule, what starts the clock and when it does not apply wins trust and the snippet.

No ranking page separates residents from visiting couples, though the official pages do (gov.gr, Athens, Chania, Heraklion). This is the single most useful fact for an Australian couple and nobody explains it.
Nobody explains that Australia does not issue a 'marriage licence', so the DFAT CNI is what Greek town halls get instead, or that the place of issue (DFAT in Australia vs Embassy Athens) can matter.
Translation rules conflict across ranking pages and even official pages (Embassy vs Ministry of Interior circulars). A careful, sourced explanation is a real gap.

No page shows the wedding-week calendar: town halls work weekdays, the file must be submitted in person, a working day is needed after a weekend wedding to register, and all of this has to fit around guest arrivals. That is our invisible-work section.

UK searchers have 6 to 30 times the AU volume for 'getting married in greece'; the Australian version is tiny but high intent. This is a consideration piece for qualified Australian couples, not a traffic play.
payload.recommended_angle: The Australian couple's honest guide to the Greek marriage licence: what the official rule actually is (one week, not eight), what starts the clock, when it does not apply to couples who live in Australia, how the DFAT CNI stands in for a 'licence', and how the paperwork, translations and town-hall visits fit into a wedding week planned from Sydney or Melbourne, with every legal line sourced to Greek or Australian government pages.
